result:
The proposed answer of 2 is wrong. The stated lower bound of Θ(n² log n) fails for i.i.d. initial data.

**Where the argument fails.** The solution claims that the slowest sine modes of the cycle have amplitude Θ(1) for ±1 initial data. This is false for i.i.d. data. The initial field is white noise, so the amplitude of the lowest mode is only about n^{-1/2}, not Θ(1). Local averaging is what matters for the range. At time t, f_t(v) is roughly an average over a window of about √t neighbours. For bounded i.i.d. data, Hoeffding's inequality shows that the range over n vertices is at most ε once the window is of size about ε⁻² log n. That needs t of order polylog(n), not n².

**Where the polynomial exponent comes from.** It comes from heavy tails. With ‖f₀‖_{L^p} ≤ 1, the largest of n i.i.d. values can be of order M = n^{1/p}. On the cycle, a spike of height M must spread over a window of width at least about M/ε before it is below ε. Diffusion takes time about M² = n^{2/p} to do this. This gives a lower bound of n^{2/p} on the cycle, which is consistent with the problem's statement that the exponent is tight for cycles. At p = 1 it gives n², matching the trivial upper bound.

This lower bound is derived heuristically, and I did not verify the matching upper bound over all graphs. The conclusion is β_p = 2/p, which depends on p. The claim that β_p is constantly 2 is incorrect.

VERDICT: REJECT
